The proxy of %1$s asks for no password, so any app on this phone can use it. Such an app can learn that you use %1$s and where its server is, and send its own traffic through it.

Off unless you turn it on. No circumvention tool is known to check which app sends UDP to its proxy: while %1$s carries UDP for Watch, other apps on this phone may send UDP through it too, even with a password. While this is off, calls and some games in the apps you send through %1$s do not work. Web pages still load.

Private DNS is set to %1$s. Android then sends the names that apps look up to %1$s itself, encrypted, past Watch and past %2$s. Your network cannot read those names, but it can see that this phone uses %1$s. And %1$s sees the names and your real address on the internet. For the apps you send through %2$s, set Private DNS to Automatic or Off.
Look for Private DNS in the settings that open. On some phones it is one step further in.

Screenshots
This app blocks screenshots and screen recordings, so that no picture of what it shows is saved or shared. If you need a screenshot to ask for help, you can allow it for one minute.
Allow screenshots for one minute
Screenshots are allowed now. They are blocked again after one minute, or as soon as you leave the app.
Block screenshots now
Apps and the VPN
Android tells every app that a VPN is on, and Watch cannot hide that. Some apps report it, and some refuse to work while a VPN is on.

If an app does not work with Watch, leave it out. It then goes to the internet without Watch: Watch does not see or record its connections, and it does not go through your circumvention tool. Android no longer tells that app its network is a VPN, but the app may still find that the phone has a VPN interface. While Watch is on, a change takes a moment, because Watch sets up its tunnel again.
